For a large sample size (n), the null distribution of the test statistic is approximately Z, so whether we use t(n - 1) or Z to calculate the p-values should not make a big difference. Here is another practical way to look at this point: if we have a large n, our sample has more information about the population. model.question: A t-test for a mean is based on a sample of $n = 15$. How many degrees of freedom does the null distribution of the test statistic have?

choices.feedback: Correct! The t-test statistic has $n - 1 = 14$ degrees of freedom.
The degrees of freedom are one LESS than the sample size.
The degrees of freedom depend on the sample size, not the number of hypotheses.

model.question: Why does using s instead of $\sigma$ change the null distribution from Z to t?

choices.text: Using s adds a second source of sample-to-sample variability, giving the statistic more spread than a z-score
choices.feedback: Correct! s varies from sample to sample, adding a second source of variability on top of x-bar's, which fattens the tails of the distribution of the statistic.

choices.text: Because s is always larger than $\sigma$
choices.feedback: s is not systematically larger than $\sigma—it$ varies around it.

choices.text: Because using s introduces a calculation error
choices.feedback: The change affects small samples most, but the reason is the extra variability, not a calculation error.
